text: PostgreSQL 16 says client authentication is controlled by the pg_hba.conf file in the cluster data directory unless hba_file points elsewhere. The file is read as one record per line. For a connection attempt, PostgreSQL uses the first record whose connection type, client address, database, and user all match. There is no fallback to later records if authentication with that first matching record fails. If no record matches at all, access is denied.

In PostgreSQL 16, a pg_hba.conf entry can be an authentication rule or an include directive. The supported include directives are include, include_if_exists, and include_dir. Included content is inserted where the directive appears. For include_dir, PostgreSQL reads files that do not start with a dot and do end with .conf, and it processes them in file-name order using C locale ordering.

PostgreSQL 16 supports local, host, hostssl, hostnossl, hostgssenc, and hostnogssenc record types. local is for Unix-domain sockets. host matches TCP/IP whether or not SSL or GSSAPI encryption is used. hostssl matches only SSL connections and requires both PostgreSQL to be built with SSL support and the ssl setting to be enabled. hostgssenc matches only GSSAPI-encrypted TCP/IP connections and requires GSSAPI support. Remote TCP/IP access also depends on listen_addresses, because the default server behavior only listens on the loopback address localhost.

In PostgreSQL 16, the database field can match all, sameuser, samerole, replication, specific database names, or regular expressions. The user field can match all, a specific user, a role name prefixed with plus, or a regular expression. For both database and user fields, a value starting with slash is treated as a regular expression, multiple names or regexes can be separated by commas, and a file prefixed with at-sign can supply names or regexes from another file.

The address field in PostgreSQL 16 can use CIDR-style IP ranges, explicit IP address plus mask columns, host names, or the keywords all, samehost, and samenet. samehost matches the server's own IP addresses, and samenet matches addresses in directly connected subnets. When a host name is used, PostgreSQL first checks reverse resolution of the client IP to a host name, then does a forward lookup of that host name to confirm the client address. A host name beginning with a dot matches a suffix such as foo.example.com.

The auth-method field selects how a matching connection is authenticated. PostgreSQL 16 lists methods including trust, reject, scram-sha-256, md5, password, gss, sspi, ident, peer, ldap, radius, cert, pam, and bsd. trust allows the connection without checking credentials, while reject blocks it unconditionally. ident is only for TCP/IP and uses the client ident service; if ident is specified for a local connection, PostgreSQL uses peer instead. peer is available only for local connections. hostssl rules can also use the clientcert option to require a trusted client certificate.

The order of pg_hba.conf records matters because PostgreSQL checks them sequentially and stops at the first matching entry. On most systems, changes to pg_hba.conf are applied after startup only when the server receives SIGHUP, for example through pg_ctl reload or pg_reload_conf(). On Microsoft Windows, new connections see file changes immediately. PostgreSQL 16 also notes that pg_hba_file_rules can help diagnose load problems, and that passing pg_hba.conf checks is not enough by itself because the user still needs CONNECT privilege on the target database.

In PostgreSQL 15, the database field can match all, sameuser, samerole, replication, specific database names, or a file prefixed with at-sign. The user field can match all users, a specific user, a role name prefixed with plus, or a file prefixed with at-sign. This older version description does not treat slash-prefixed database or user values as regular expressions.

Streaming replication allows a primary server to continuously stream WAL records to one or more standby servers. Standby servers can be configured as read-only query destinations while applying WAL changes. Synchronous replication, when enabled, waits for at least one standby to confirm receipt of each WAL record before the primary commits the transaction. Asynchronous replication does not wait; it provides lower latency at the risk of potential data loss on primary failure.

Replication slots are a feature that prevents the primary server from removing WAL segments before all standbys have received them. A slot tracks consumer progress via the restart_lsn. If a standby disconnects, the primary retains WAL until the standby reconnects and consumes the backlog, or until the slot is dropped. Without slots, administrators must manually monitor WAL retention via wal_keep_size. Slots are configured via pg_create_physical_replication_slot or pg_create_logical_replication_slot.

Hot standby allows read-only queries on a standby server while it continuously applies WAL from the primary. Queries see a snapshot of the database as of the WAL apply position. Long-running queries on the standby can conflict with WAL records that need to update the same rows; in that case, the query is canceled (with conflict resolution tunable per operation type via hot_standby_feedback and max_standby_streaming_delay). This is the foundation for read-scaling with replicas.

Failover is the unplanned promotion of a standby to primary when the original primary has failed. Switchover is a planned handoff for maintenance. PostgreSQL does not include built-in automatic failover; it requires external tools such as Patroni, repmgr, or Pacemaker. After failover, the old primary must be reconfigured as a standby of the new primary, otherwise split-brain can occur. The pg_ctl promote command performs a manual promotion.

Replication conflicts occur when a standby applies WAL that conflicts with a query running on the standby. The most common causes are: row-level conflicts when WAL modifies a row the standby query is reading, lock conflicts when WAL acquires a lock the standby query holds, and table-space conflicts. The default behavior is to cancel the query when the conflict is detected. The max_standby_streaming_delay parameter controls how long the WAL apply waits for the query to finish before canceling.

Logical replication replicates data at the granularity of tables and rows, in contrast to physical replication which replicates entire database files. Logical replication uses publications on the publisher and subscriptions on the subscriber. It allows selective replication of individual tables, replication across different PostgreSQL major versions, and bidirectional replication for multi-master setups. Conflicts on the subscriber side must be resolved by the application or by conflict-resolution triggers.

Declarative partitioning in PostgreSQL uses the PARTITION BY clause of CREATE TABLE to divide a table into smaller physical pieces. PostgreSQL supports partitioning by RANGE, LIST, and HASH. Each partition is itself a table that stores a subset of the parent table's data. Queries that filter on the partition key can use partition pruning to skip irrelevant partitions entirely, dramatically reducing I/O. The partitioning structure is enforced via partition constraints.

Partition pruning is the query optimizer's ability to skip scanning partitions that cannot contain matching rows. Pruning is enabled when the query's WHERE clause contains a constant expression on the partition key. RANGE and LIST partitioning benefit most from pruning; HASH partitioning does not benefit because each row maps to a fixed bucket regardless of query pattern. The planner's enable_partition_pruning parameter controls this behavior.

ALTER TABLE ATTACH PARTITION adds an existing table to a partitioned parent as a new partition. The table must have a constraint that exactly matches the partition boundary; otherwise the attachment fails. ALTER TABLE DETACH PARTITION removes a partition back to a standalone table. These operations are metadata-only when the partition is empty and may require a full table scan when the partition contains data. Concurrent operations on the parent table are blocked during the scan.

Each partition is a separate physical table, so an index created on the parent table is automatically created on every existing partition. New indexes must be created ON the parent table to be propagated to all partitions. A query plan that uses an index on the parent table will scan only the relevant partitions (after pruning) and use the index on each scanned partition. Local indexes are partition-scoped; global indexes that span partitions are not supported in PostgreSQL.

A DEFAULT partition in PostgreSQL's LIST and RANGE partitioned tables holds rows that do not match any other partition's bound. The default partition is created via PARTITION OF ... DEFAULT. Inserts that do not match any specific partition go to the default. The planner scans the default partition when the partition key is not pruned. It is a common operational error to leave the default partition unbounded, leading to silent accumulation of misrouted rows.

PostgreSQL configuration parameters can be set in postgresql.conf, on the command line via -c, or for the current session via SET. ALTER SYSTEM writes to postgresql.auto.conf, which is merged with postgresql.conf at startup. Parameters can be marked as PGC_INTERNAL (compile-time), PGC_POSTMASTER (requires server restart), PGC_SIGHUP (requires SIGHUP signal), or PGC_S_USER (per-session). The classification determines when a change takes effect.

A SIGHUP signal (e.g., pg_ctl reload) causes PostgreSQL to re-read postgresql.conf and postgresql.auto.conf. Only PGC_SIGHUP parameters can be changed this way. Parameters of class PGC_POSTMASTER require a full server restart to take effect. There is no way to reload everything; the server checks each parameter's class and only updates those that allow SIGHUP. AUTOCOMMIT-style settings and most planner tunables are SIGHUP-friendly; shared_buffers and wal_level are not.

PostgreSQL supports four scopes for parameter settings: USER (per-session), SUPERUSER (per-session, requires superuser), DATABASE (per-database, persistent), and SYSTEM (system-wide, persistent). The SET command sets USER scope for the current session. To make a session-level change persistent across connections, use ALTER ROLE x SET parameter = value or ALTER DATABASE x SET parameter = value. The pg_settings view shows the current effective value and source of every parameter.

The log_statement parameter controls which SQL statements are written to the server log. Allowed values are none (no logging), ddl (only DDL like CREATE, ALTER, DROP), mod (DDL plus INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), and all (every statement including SELECT). Setting log_statement without enabling log_line_prefix may produce logs that are hard to parse. The logs go to stderr by default; redirect via logging_collector.

The pg_settings view exposes every PostgreSQL configuration parameter along with its current value, source file, and min/max bounds. SELECT name, setting, unit, source FROM pg_settings WHERE category = 'Connections' is a common starting query. The RESET command restores a parameter to its default value. The 'source' column indicates whether the value came from postgresql.conf, ALTER SYSTEM, the command line, or a session-local SET.

The scram-sha-256 authentication method uses the Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM) with SHA-256. It is the recommended default for password authentication in PostgreSQL 14 and later. SCRAM provides mutual authentication and is resistant to replay attacks, dictionary attacks, and man-in-the-middle attacks. The server stores the verifier (not the password itself) and the client must supply the password during the SCRAM exchange.

The md5 authentication method uses a custom challenge-response protocol with the MD5 hash of the password. It is older than SCRAM and is considered less secure because it is vulnerable to replay attacks on the same connection. PostgreSQL 14 deprecated md5 in favor of scram-sha-256. Existing md5-verifier entries can be migrated to SCRAM via the postgres user's ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD '...' command, which re-encrypts the stored verifier.

The peer authentication method obtains the client's operating-system user name from the kernel and uses it as the database user name. It is available only on local connections (Unix-domain sockets). The OS-to-database mapping is configured via the pg_ident.conf file. peer is a common single-sign-on mechanism for local development: the OS user 'alice' connects as PostgreSQL role 'alice' without a password prompt.

The ident authentication method uses the IDENT protocol (RFC 1413) to look up the OS user from a TCP/IP connection and map it to a PostgreSQL role via pg_ident.conf. ident is only available for TCP/IP connections. On local connections, peer is used instead. ident is generally less secure than peer because it relies on an external service (typically running on port 113) that may be spoofed.

GSSAPI authentication uses the Generic Security Services Application Program Interface (GSSAPI) to perform Kerberos 5 authentication. It is the standard for single-sign-on in enterprise environments. Configuration requires setting krb_server_keyfile and ensuring that the postgres service principal is registered with the Kerberos KDC. The pg_ident.conf file can map GSSAPI principal names to PostgreSQL roles.

PostgreSQL uses the concept of roles to manage database access permissions. A role can be either a user (with LOGIN privilege) or a group (without LOGIN). CREATE ROLE alice LOGIN creates a login-capable role. Roles can be members of other roles (group membership) via GRANT role1 TO role2. The bootstrap superuser is created at initdb time and named 'postgres' by default.

GRANT is used to give privileges on database objects to roles. Privileges include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, CREATE, CONNECT, TEMPORARY, EXECUTE, USAGE, and SET. GRANT can be applied to specific tables, schemas, or globally. WITH GRANT OPTION allows the grantee to grant that privilege to others. REVOKE removes privileges.

A role can be a member of other roles. CREATE ROLE managers NOLOGIN; GRANT managers TO alice; -- alice is now in 'managers' group. SET ROLE managers -- alice can now use the managers' privileges. SET ROLE NONE restores the original role. The session_user is the original login role; current_user changes with SET ROLE. INHERIT is a default role attribute that allows automatic inheritance of privileges without SET ROLE.

PostgreSQL log output goes to stderr by default. With logging_collector enabled, the server redirects log output to files in the log_directory and rotates them via log_rotation_age and log_rotation_size. syslog on Unix or eventlog on Windows can be selected via log_destination. The csvlog format is preferred for downstream parsing because each log line is a single CSV row with structured fields.

The log_line_prefix parameter specifies a printf-style format string that is prepended to every log line. Common escape sequences include %t (timestamp), %u (user name), %d (database name), %p (process ID), %r (remote host), %a (application name). Without a prefix, the log lines are extremely hard to parse with downstream tools. A typical production setting is log_line_prefix = '%t [%p]: user=%u,db=%d,app=%a '.

log_min_duration_statement logs any SQL statement that runs for at least the specified number of milliseconds. It is the primary tool for performance diagnostics. Setting it to 0 logs every statement (high volume); setting it to a small value (e.g., 250ms) captures only slow queries. The log entry includes the parameter values of the statement, which is useful for slow-query analysis but may leak sensitive data if the logs are not protected.

pg_basebackup creates a binary copy of the running database cluster. It works with the streaming replication protocol to take a consistent snapshot without blocking writes. The output can be a tar archive (-Ft) or a plain directory. Use -X stream to include the WAL files needed for recovery. pg_basebackup is the foundation for setting up a new standby server.

pg_dump produces a logical backup of a single database as a SQL script or a custom-format archive. The script can be replayed with psql to recreate the database. The custom-format (-Fc) supports parallel restore via pg_restore and selective restore of individual tables. pg_dump is online (does not block reads or writes) and is the standard tool for migrations and small-to-medium backups.

Streaming replication in PostgreSQL 15 allows a primary server to stream WAL records to standby servers. Asynchronous replication is the default; synchronous waits for standby confirmation. Note: Replication slots were promoted from experimental to stable in PostgreSQL 11 but with different default behavior than later versions.
